title: Cold standby bootstrap — latency impact analysis and ops checklist
content:
Summary:

This is the notes + checklist from our 2025-02-25 cold-standby bootstrapping experiment (region: eu-west-1 -> cold pool in us-west-2). Goal: quantify tail latency and operational steps when we need to bring cold GPU capacity fully online and route traffic to it, and capture what needs to be codified into runbooks. This doc is intentionally informal — scratchpad for oncall and SRE triage.

Motivation / context:
- Warm standby (kvcache preseeded) has clear benefits but is expensive for low-traffic tenants. For some customers and cost tiers we still rely on cold pools (idle instances that must boot from image and load weights).
- Previous incidents showed a surprise spike in 99th token latency during a multi-region evacuation when many cold servers were booted at once. We ran a focused sim to measure: GPU init time, model load time, first-response latency distribution, and the effect of staggered traffic ramp strategies.

Experiment summary (2025-02-25 02:00 UTC):
- Trigger: scripted boot of 24 cold nodes in us-west-2, stagger windows of 0s (parallel), 30s, and 120s.
- Model: redwood-v1-7b-8k (float16 default), sequence length profile: median 256, 95th 1024.
- Obs ingestion: small steady traffic (10 rps) directed to new nodes via internal weighted routing for the first 10m, then ramp to 100 rps over 15m.
- Measurement points: node ready event, model loaded, first token out, 50th token out, GPU memory available, kv-cache warm ratio.

Key observations:
- Cold boot timeline (median numbers):
  - Instance boot (OS up, kube ready): 48s (range 36–72s)
  - Container start + runtime init: 12s (9–18s)
  - Model file load to GPU (over EBS): 42s (28–86s) — large variance due to EBS throughput and parallel loads
  - JIT/kernel warmups and first-inference overhead: 1.5s (0.6–5.2s)
  - End-to-end first-token latency for 256-token requests: median 1.9s (p99 6.8s) when model load done; if request arrives during model load, first-token is dominated by model load and request sees 45–120s latency (depends whether request queued or retried).
- Parallel boot (24 at once) created a short-lived EBS bandwidth saturation pattern; many nodes had model load stretched to >90s. Staggering 30s reduced p99 by ~20%; staggering 120s reduced p99 by ~45% and smoothed I/O bursts.
- KV cache: 0% warm on boot by definition. Replaying 1 hour of observed prefixes warmed ~40% after 10m of traffic on a single node. Early requests suffered increased compute cost until cache hit ratios rose.
- Routing behaviors: when traffic is routed to nodes still model-loading, requests either queued in front proxy (bad: increases tail), or immediately failed over to fallback model (good: sacrifices cost/quality). Our current routing policy uses a short kube-readiness probe which flips ready=true before model fully loaded — triggers traffic to unready-for-inference nodes.

Immediate operational recommendations (short term):
1) Adjust readiness probe: differentiate kube ready vs inference-ready. New probe endpoint /health/inference-ready that returns OK only after model loaded and a short self-check inference returns within latency bound.
2) Implement staged model pulls: use a coordinator to gate model pulls to N concurrent pulls per availability zone (configurable, default 4) to avoid EBS saturation during large scale boots.
3) Update routing policy: prefer removing nodes from active weights until inference-ready. If node is not inference-ready, route to fallback pool (lower-cost fallback or queued).
4) Traffic ramp template: recommended ramp = {initial: 5% traffic -> wait 5m -> 20% -> wait 10m -> 100% over next 10m} for >20 node bring-ups; operator override allowed. Attach a standard curl-based check to each step.
5) KV cache pre-warm option: provide customers a pre-warm hook that replays recent prefixes to cold pool on controlled schedule. Not default but available for pay tiers.

Operator checklist (quick items during a cold pool boot event):
- Pre-checks (before boot trigger):
  - Confirm target AZ capacity available: aws console / internal capacity dashboard
  - Confirm EBS throughput allocation for model-store; raise iops if planning parallel pulls >8
  - Open incident channel: #ops-oncall and tag infra leads
- During boot (parallel or staggered):
  - Monitor model_load: prometheus metric model_load_seconds (per-node)
  - Watch EBS queue length and throttling metrics
  - Ensure inference-ready probe flips to true only after first successful sample inference (check /internal/checks/sample-inference)
  - If >10% nodes stuck in model_load >90s: pause scheduling new boots, reduce concurrent pulls (operator: /bin/scheduler scale-down-pulls 2)
- After boot completes:
  - Validate tail latency (p95/p99) on routing edge (region loadbalancer metrics)
  - Run small canary workload to verify kv-cache behavior; if quality regressions detected, enable fallback routing to warm pool
  - Label nodes with boot_swarm_id for future forensic queries

Rollback and mitigation playbook (if latency > SLOs):
- Immediate: shift traffic back to originating region or to warm dedicated pool via traffic weights (rollback window 60s)
- If rollback fails (capacity constraints): increase fallback-model weight, enable degraded-quality gates, notify CS for customers with strict SLAs
- Post-incident: collect model_load histograms, EBS throttling traces, kube events, and attach to INF ticket.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Is the model store better served by a caching proxy (e.g., s3 gateway) near the nodes to reduce EBS pressure? Tradeoffs: complexity vs isolation. Owner: Marco Li (INF-2189).
- Can we formalize an "inference-ready" lifecycle in the node informer and surface to autoscaler? Owner: Evan (INF-2191).
- Cost model: what is the breakeven for warm vs cold for typical customer load shapes? Analytics needed. Owner: Priya (ENG-ops).

Notes to self / rough ideas (raw):
- Might be worth offering an "on-demand prefetch" API: user kicks a prefetch job to warm a given model in a region for X hours.
- Investigate sharding model files across multiple smaller EBS volumes to parallelize reads.
- Add chaos test to k6 harness: simulate 50% of nodes cold & route 30% traffic over 30m; assert p99 < 5s for first-token for sequence <=512.

References and artifacts:
- INF-2123 (incident log): https://redwood.atlassian.net/browse/INF-2123
- Infra PR implementing model_load histogram: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/876
- Slack thread: #ops-oncall (2025-02-25): https://slack.com/archives/C01234567/p1676001234567890

Next steps (actionable):
- Evan: prototype inference-ready probe and follow-up PR (due 2025-03-10)
- Marco: test coordinator for staged pulls; run lab with 100 nodes (due 2025-03-20)
- Priya: run cost breakeven analysis across customer cohorts and propose tiering (due 2025-03-07)
- Aisha: convert checklist items into a short runbook page and add to oncall runbook (due 2025-03-05)

Unresolved: how to signal to external routing layers (external DNS, CDN) — need to align with product on acceptable outage windows for DNS TTL reductions.

End of notes.
